chapter_title: Understanding Actors, Components, and the Level Editor
chapter_summary:
Building upon our introduction to the Unreal Editor, let's dive deeper into the fundamental building blocks of your game world: **Actors** and **Components**. These two concepts are absolutely central to how everything works in Unreal Engine, and understanding their relationship is key to effective game development. Simply put, an **Actor** is anything that can be placed into your game level. Think of it as a container. This could be a static mesh (like a chair or a wall), a light source, a camera, a player character, or even an invisible trigger volume. Actors have a transform (location, rotation, scale) and can be manipulated directly in the Viewport.

However, an Actor itself is often quite basic. To give an Actor functionality, we attach **Components** to it. Components are modular pieces of functionality that can be added to any Actor. For example, a `StaticMeshComponent` gives an Actor a visual 3D model. A `PointLightComponent` makes an Actor emit light. A `CameraComponent` allows an Actor to act as a camera. A `MovementComponent` enables an Actor to move around. The power of Components lies in their reusability and modularity. You can combine different Components on a single Actor to create complex behaviors. For instance, a basic lamp Actor might have a `StaticMeshComponent` for its visual model and a `PointLightComponent` to emit light. Your player character Actor might have a `SkeletalMeshComponent` for its animated model, a `CapsuleComponent` for collision, and a `CharacterMovementComponent` to handle its locomotion.

This creates a hierarchical structure: an Actor is the root, and Components are attached to it. Components can even have other Components attached to them, forming a tree-like structure. When you move, rotate, or scale an Actor, all its attached Components (and their children) move, rotate, and scale along with it. This parent-child relationship is incredibly powerful for organizing complex objects. For example, if you have a car Actor, its wheels, doors, and lights could all be child Actors or Components. Moving the car's root Actor would move the entire vehicle. You can see this hierarchy clearly in the **Details Panel** under the "Components" tab, and also in the **World Outliner** if you expand an Actor's entry.

Let's consider how to work with Actors and Components in the Level Editor. You can add Actors to your level in several ways. The simplest is often dragging them from the **Content Browser** (for assets like `Static Meshes` or `Skeletal Meshes`) or from the **Place Actors** panel (found under the Modes panel on the left side of the editor). The Place Actors panel is particularly useful for common Actor types like `Lights` (Point Light, Spot Light, Directional Light), `Cameras`, `Volumes` (like `Trigger Volume` or `Blocking Volume`), and basic geometric primitives.

Once an Actor is in your level, you'll frequently need to adjust its position, rotation, and scale precisely. We've already touched upon the `W`, `E`, `R` keys for basic transformations. However, the editor offers more advanced tools for accuracy. **Snapping** is one such feature. You can enable grid snapping (for movement), angle snapping (for rotation), and scale snapping (for scaling) using the icons in the Viewport toolbar. For example, grid snapping ensures that when you move an object, it aligns perfectly with the editor's grid, making it easier to line up walls or floor tiles. Angle snapping rotates objects by fixed increments (e.g., 15 or 45 degrees), which is great for ensuring symmetrical rotations.

Another important concept is the **Pivot Point**. Every Actor has a pivot point, which is the origin around which transformations (rotation and scaling) occur. By default, this is often the center or bottom-center of the Actor's bounding box. Sometimes, you'll need to temporarily change the pivot point for precise manipulation. You can do this by holding `Alt` and middle-clicking (or `Ctrl + Alt` and middle-clicking for a persistent pivot) to move the pivot to a different location. This is incredibly useful when you need to rotate an object around a specific edge or corner, rather than its geometric center. For instance, rotating a door around its hinge rather than its middle.

Common mistakes often involve forgetting the parent-child hierarchy. If you attach a light to a character and then move the light independently, it will detach from the character's movement. Always ensure your desired components are correctly parented. Another common issue is not using snapping when precision is needed, leading to misaligned geometry and visual glitches. Always consider the context: for organic environments, snapping might be less critical, but for architectural elements, it's indispensable. Mastering Actors, Components, and the transformation tools will give you the foundational control needed to build compelling and well-structured game levels.

screens.title: Actors, Components, and the Level Editor
screens.subtitle: How the scene is built from containers and modular parts, and how to position them precisely

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn how Unreal’s world is constructed from two related ideas: Actors and Components. An Actor is any object you place or spawn in a level — a container with a transform. Components are modular pieces you attach to that container to give it visuals, collision, sensing, movement, or lights. Understanding this distinction is the first step to building robust scenes. You will see how attaching a light component to a mesh makes the light move with the mesh, and how parenting in the World Outliner enforces the same rules. You’ll also learn practical editor skills: adding Actors from the Place Actors panel or Content Browser, using the transform gizmo for movement, and using snapping and pivot adjustments for precise placement. By the end of the chapter you’ll be able to compose compound objects like a lamp or a vehicle from reusable components and place them with pixel-perfect alignment. Keep an eye out for common mistakes such as forgetting to parent components or skipping snapping when building architectural geometry.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Actors are containers with transforms; Components attach to Actors to add modular behavior and visuals. Together they form the scene hierarchy you manipulate in the Level Editor.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives frame the practical skills you will practice in the Level Editor. First, you will be able to tell the difference between an Actor and a Component and explain why that relationship matters for scene composition. This helps you design reusable, maintainable objects. Second, you will add and configure common Actor types such as Static Mesh Actors and Light Actors, so you can populate a level with visible geometry and correct lighting. The third objective focuses on attaching and detaching Components: you will attach a Spot Light Component to a mesh and observe how it becomes part of that Actor’s hierarchy. Finally, you will master the advanced transform tools: snapping, pivot points, and parent-child transforms so you can align architecture and animate hinged objects without drift. Each objective is paired with a competency milestone so you can verify your understanding by building small test cases in the editor.

screens.title: Actors vs Components — a clear definition
screens.subtitle: Actors are containers with transforms; Components add capability

narration.text: Let's define the two foundational terms clearly. An Actor is any object you place or spawn into a level that possesses a transform: location, rotation, and scale. Think of an Actor as a labeled container or entity that the editor tracks and can serialize. It can represent anything from a simple static mesh to a camera or a player pawn. A Component is a modular piece of functionality that you attach to an Actor. Components give Actors visuals, physics, collision, lighting, or movement handling. For example, a StaticMeshComponent provides geometry and collision. A PointLightComponent emits light. A CharacterMovementComponent implements movement rules. The strength of Components is their reusability: the same StaticMeshComponent class can be attached to many Actors with different meshes and settings. A common misconception is to treat Actors as behavior-rich on their own; in Unreal most runtime behavior comes from Components or Actor-level scripts that use Components. Another important point is that Components can be nested to form a tree under an Actor; child components inherit transform changes when the root Actor moves. An example: a lamp Actor that contains a StaticMeshComponent for the lamp body and a PointLightComponent for the glow. Moving the lamp Actor moves both parts together. To test your understanding, create a small Actor, add a visible StaticMeshComponent and then add a Spot Light Component; adjust the Spot Light’s intensity and color to see how the Component directly alters the Actor’s appearance. How does thinking in containers plus modules change how you design scene objects?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Actor = container with transform. Component = reusable module that gives the Actor visuals or behavior.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Actors vs Components
Actor — the container
An object that can be placed or spawned; stores a transform and references to its Components.
Example: a Static Mesh Actor named "Lamp_01" placed in the level.
Behavior note: Actors can hold scripts or Blueprints that manage Components.
Misconception: Actors alone usually aren't the granular unit of functionality — Components provide that.
Component — modular capability
Attach one or many Components to an Actor to give it a mesh, a light, collision, or movement.
Example: StaticMeshComponent, PointLightComponent, CameraComponent.
Tip: reuse Components across Actors for consistent behavior and easier maintenance.
Check: add a Spot Light Component to a wall Actor and observe it listed in the Components tab.
Analogy: Actor is a toy robot; Components are the robot's battery, speaker, and wheels — remove or replace a component to change capability.
Key Takeaway
Design objects as containers plus modular components to keep scenes flexible and predictable.

screens.title: Hierarchy: How parent-child transforms behave
screens.subtitle: When you move a parent, its children follow — and what that implies for design

narration.text: Hierarchy in Unreal creates a transform inheritance chain. The root Actor or component is the parent; anything nested beneath becomes a child and inherits movement, rotation, and scale changes from the parent. This is powerful for composing multi-part objects: a vehicle can be a single Actor with wheel Components or child Actors; moving the vehicle root moves the entire assembly. But hierarchy also creates coupling: rotating a parent rotates all children relative to the parent's pivot and orientation. A practical example is parenting a chair to a table: the chair becomes a child and will move when the table moves. If you rotate the chair itself, it rotates in the table’s local space which can be surprising unless you understand local versus world transforms. A common mistake is to forget parenting and move the child independently, leaving it orphaned from expected motion. Another subtle point: Components are shown inside the Details Panel and Actor entries appear in the World Outliner. Use the Outliner drag to change parentage between Actors, and use the Components tab to reorder or reparent components under the same Actor. For complex objects, keep the root Actor minimal and attach clear, named Components so you can script or animate specific parts without affecting the whole. How will you name and group components to make future edits simple?

keyIdea.title: Hierarchy insight
keyIdea.text: Parent transforms propagate to children. Use parenting intentionally to move assemblies and avoid accidental detachment.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Parent-Child Relationship
How transforms flow through the tree
A parent’s transform applies to all children; children maintain local offsets.
Example: Car Actor (root) with wheel Components. Moving the car translates every wheel automatically.
Misconception: Child rotation is in world space — actually it is relative to the parent unless you explicitly use world transform operations.
Practice: Drag one Actor on top of another in the World Outliner to make it a child. Move the parent to confirm inheritance.
Visual checklist
  • Child inherits translate, rotate, scale.
  • Rename children for clarity (Wheel_FL, Door_R).
  • Use Outliner to reparent Actors quickly.
Key Takeaway

Plan hierarchy to make group movement and targeted animation straightforward; avoid accidental detachment by confirming parentage after drag-and-drop operations.

screens.title: Common Component types and their roles
screens.subtitle: StaticMesh, Light, Camera, Collision, and Movement components

narration.text: Components are the practical building blocks you will attach to Actors to produce visuals, physics, or behavior. The most common ones you’ll encounter are StaticMeshComponent for visible, non-animated geometry; SkeletalMeshComponent for animated characters; PointLightComponent, SpotLightComponent, and DirectionalLight components for lighting; CameraComponent for viewpoint control; and collision components such as CapsuleComponent, BoxComponent, or SphereComponent. Movement-related components like CharacterMovementComponent or PawnMovementComponent implement locomotion rules for Pawn and Character Actors. Each component exposes properties in the Details panel. For instance, a PointLightComponent lets you set intensity, color, and attenuation radius. A collision component defines how the Actor interacts with physics and overlaps, and can be tuned for channels and responses. A concrete example: a player Actor might include a CapsuleComponent for collision, a SkeletalMeshComponent for the visible character, a CameraComponent attached to the head bone, and a CharacterMovementComponent to handle walking and jumping. A frequent misconception is to duplicate features across Actors rather than reusing Components — prefer attaching shared components or creating component-based Blueprints to avoid duplicate settings. Try adding a Spot Light Component to an existing wall Actor and tweak its cone angle; this will make the component’s effect visible immediately in the viewport and illustrate how Components alter the Actor’s runtime behavior.

keyIdea.title: Component roles
keyIdea.text: Each Component class provides a focused capability. Combine them to create complex Actor behavior while keeping each piece reusable.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Common Component Types
Components you will use daily
StaticMeshComponent — supplies visible geometry and collision for static objects.
SkeletalMeshComponent — used for animated characters and rigged objects.
Light Components — Point, Spot, Directional. Configure intensity and range in Details.
Collision Components — Capsule, Box, Sphere. Define physics and overlap behavior.
Movement Components — CharacterMovementComponent for player locomotion and jumping.
Quick examples
Lamp Actor = StaticMeshComponent + PointLightComponent.
Enemy Pawn = SkeletalMeshComponent + CapsuleComponent + MovementComponent.
Security Camera = StaticMeshComponent + CameraComponent.
Key Takeaway

Choose components to match single responsibilities: visuals, collision, sensing, or movement. Compose them to construct the Actor you need.

screens.title: Where to get Actors: Place Actors & Content Browser
screens.subtitle: Different workflows to add assets and common Actor types available by default

narration.text: There are two common workflows to add Actors into your level. The Place Actors panel provides quick drag-and-drop access to commonly used Actor types: lights, cameras, volumes, and basic geometry primitives. It’s optimized for building a scene quickly. The Content Browser lets you drag specific assets—Static Meshes and Skeletal Meshes—into the level as Actors that have their corresponding Components already set up. For example, dragging an SM_Wall asset from Starter Content creates a Static Mesh Actor containing a StaticMeshComponent referencing the wall asset. Place Actors is great when you need a light or a primitive quickly; Content Browser is best when you need a specific mesh from your project. A useful habit is to enable grid snapping when you drag geometry from the Content Browser, which prevents small offsets when placing floors and walls. Another common issue is accidentally creating duplicate Actors by dragging repeatedly; check the World Outliner to confirm you only have the intended instances. Practice both flows: place a Point Light from the Place Actors panel, then drag an SM_Floor_400x400 from the Content Browser and position it so it sits exactly at world origin. This reinforces how the editor creates Actor instances from either library of building blocks.

keyIdea.title: Sources of Actors
keyIdea.text: Use Place Actors for common types and the Content Browser for specific assets; both create Actor instances you place in the world.

Good for: Point Light, Spot Light, Directional Light, Primitive shapes.
Tip: Use Place Actors when prototyping a level layout because it's quick to manipulate common types.

Practice: Drag SM_Floor_400x400 to origin then enable grid snapping to align edges perfectly.

Drag a Point Light from Place Actors and a floor mesh from Content Browser. Use grid snapping to ensure the floor sits at 0,0,0 and the light is centered above it.

screens.title: Add Actors and configure them
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step workflow to place, name, and set basic properties

narration.text: Follow a consistent workflow when adding Actors to keep your level organized. Step 1: Choose your source — Place Actors for primitives or the Content Browser for project assets. Step 2: Drag the asset into the Viewport and set its initial transform. Step 3: Give the Actor a descriptive name in the World Outliner, for example SM_Floor_Main or Lamp_Entrance. Step 4: Open the Details Panel and inspect which Components exist. Static Mesh Actors will include a StaticMeshComponent; Lights will include a LightComponent. Step 5: Tweak properties — a light’s intensity, color, and attenuation radius; a mesh’s collision and mobility (static, stationary, movable). Step 6: Test the Actor by moving the camera around in the Viewport and toggling relevant properties to confirm expected behavior. An example sequence: drag SM_Floor_400x400, snap it to the grid at (0,0,0), drag SM_Wall_400x200 and position it using rotation and grid snapping, then drag a Point Light and raise it to the ceiling. A common mistake is leaving Actors with default names; renaming saves time later when you search or script behaviors. After configuration, save the level to persist your placements.

keyIdea.title: Action plan
keyIdea.text: Use a repeatable add→name→inspect→configure→test cycle to keep levels organized and predictable.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Add & Configure Actors
Step-by-step
  1. Choose Place Actors or Content Browser.
  2. Drag asset into Viewport; set transform with W/E/R.
  3. Rename Actor in World Outliner for clarity.
  4. Open Details Panel to inspect Components and properties.
  5. Adjust mobility, collision, light intensity, and color as needed.
  6. Test in-viewport and save level.
Practical tips
Rename objects immediately to prevent confusion during later edits.
Set mobility correctly: static for level geometry, movable for animated objects and lights when needed.
Use Details Panel filters to find exact Component properties quickly.
Example
Place a floor, snap to origin, place walls with grid snapping, add a Point Light and set attenuation so the room is evenly lit. Rename objects to Floor_Main, Wall_North, Light_Ceiling.

screens.title: Inspecting structure and properties
screens.subtitle: Where to see Components and manage Actor hierarchy

narration.text: Two Editor panels are essential to inspect and manage Actors: the World Outliner and the Details Panel. The World Outliner shows all Actors in the level in a hierarchical tree. Expand an Actor to see any child Actors you parented. Use it to rename, reparent, or select objects quickly. The Details Panel shows the selected Actor’s properties and its Components tab. In the Components section you can add new Components, reorder them, or select an individual Component to edit its properties. For example, selecting a wall Actor and expanding Components will reveal a StaticMeshComponent entry. Selecting that component allows you to change the mesh asset, tweak collision, or add a Spot Light Component. A frequent error is adding a component to the wrong Actor; always confirm the Actor name in the Details Panel header before adding. Another useful technique is toggling viewport visibility or collision visibility from the Outliner to debug overlapping geometry. Concrete workflow: select an Actor in the Viewport, look to Details to find its Components, click Add Component to attach a Spot Light Component, then change the Spot Light’s cone angle and intensity to see live updates. These panels are where you inspect and verify the structure and configuration of every Actor you place.

keyIdea.title: Inspection hubs
keyIdea.text: Use World Outliner for hierarchy and Details Panel to view/edit Components and actor properties.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Details Panel & World Outliner
World Outliner
See every Actor in the level, reparent children, and rename items for clarity.
  • Drag an Actor onto another to make it a child.
  • Use search to find objects by name.
Details Panel
Inspect properties and the Components list for the selected Actor. Add or configure Components here.
Example: expand Components on a wall Actor to find StaticMeshComponent and Add Component → Spot Light.
Tip: Confirm selected Actor name in the Details header before adding components to avoid accidental attachments.
Check
After adding a component, move the parent Actor and confirm the new component follows. If it doesn't, re-open Outliner and verify parentage.

screens.title: Attaching and detaching Components
screens.subtitle: How to add functionality to an Actor and remove it safely

narration.text: Attaching and detaching Components is how you modify an Actor’s functionality without recreating the whole Actor. To attach a Component, select your Actor, open the Details Panel, and use Add Component to pick the component class you want. For example, add a Spot Light Component to an SM_Wall Actor to create a mounted light. Once attached, the new component appears in the Components list and you can select it to change its properties. To detach or remove a component, select it within the Components list and remove it; this will remove that functionality from the Actor. A practical example: create a Lamp Actor with a StaticMeshComponent and add a PointLightComponent. To experiment, try detaching the PointLightComponent and see the lighting update immediately. A common pitfall is adding a Component to the wrong Actor; always confirm the selected Actor’s name before adding. Another important practice is to save your Blueprint or Actor changes after you modify components, especially if the Actor is part of a reusable Blueprint class. If you need to move a component to a different Actor, you often re-add it to the target Actor and copy property values rather than attempting to drag a component between separate Actor instances. This workflow keeps your scene stable and predictable while enabling rapid iteration.

keyIdea.title: Attach safely
keyIdea.text: Add Components via the Details Panel to extend functionality; remove them to revert behavior. Confirm selection before changing hierarchy.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Attaching & Detaching Components
Add Component workflow
  1. Select Actor in Viewport or Outliner.
  2. Open Details Panel and choose Add Component.
  3. Pick the component type and configure properties.
  4. Save changes to Blueprint or level as needed.
Remove or move
To remove: select the component entry in Components list and delete it. To emulate moving, add the same component to the target Actor and copy settings.
Avoid trying to drag components between separate Actor instances; reattach and set properties intentionally.
Example
Attach a Spot Light Component to a wall Actor. Change the cone angle and intensity, then delete it to observe the immediate effect in the viewport.

screens.title: W, E, R — Move, Rotate, Scale
screens.subtitle: Understanding the transform gizmo and how it controls object placement

narration.text: The transform gizmo is the visual manipulator you use to move, rotate, and scale selected Actors. Press W for translate, E for rotate, and R for scale to switch gizmo modes. The gizmo shows axis handles that allow constrained operations along single axes and plane handles for two-axis operations. Translation arrows move the Actor in local or world space depending on your transform mode. Rotations are performed around the Actor’s pivot point — an important relationship because pivot placement determines the center of rotation and scaling. Use the gizmo to nudge objects precisely while watching the Details Panel for exact transform values. A practical example: select a wall and press E to rotate it exactly 90 degrees using angle snapping. A common misconception is assuming scaling and rotation always use world axes; many operations default to local axes relative to the Actor’s current orientation. If you need world-space transformations, change the transform mode in the toolbar. Practice reading the transform numbers in the Details Panel and entering precise values when snapping is insufficient. The gizmo, combined with snapping and pivot tools, gives you precise control over all Actor placements in the scene.

keyIdea.title: Gizmo control
keyIdea.text: Use W/E/R to switch transform modes. Pivot location and axis mode (local/world) determine how transforms apply.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Transform Gizmo
Gizmo basics
W = move, E = rotate, R = scale. Use axis handles for constrained transformations.
Local vs world axes: toggle transform mode in the toolbar to change behavior.
Check numeric transforms in Details for precise edits.
Practice prompt
Rotate a door 90 degrees using E with angle snapping enabled. If rotation looks off, check the pivot position to ensure it rotates around the hinge.
Key Takeaway
Control transforms with W/E/R and confirm axis and pivot settings to avoid unexpected motions.

screens.title: Snapping: grid, angle, and scale
screens.subtitle: Use snapping to ensure precise alignment and avoid gaps

narration.text: Snapping enforces discrete increments for transforms so objects align predictably. Grid snapping constrains translation to the editor grid; angle snapping rotates objects by fixed increments such as 15 or 45 degrees; and scale snapping snaps uniform or axis scale values. Enable these snapping options from the Viewport toolbar. A concrete example: when constructing a room with SM_Floor and SM_Wall assets, enable grid snapping with a grid size equal to your mesh dimensions so walls meet perfectly without gaps. For rotation, angle snapping keeps objects symmetrical and prevents tiny offsets that cause visual seams. Scale snapping is less commonly used but helpful when scaling multiple tiles to consistent sizes. A common mistake is leaving snapping off while placing modular architecture; this leads to invisible seams or lighting artifacts from misaligned geometry. Another tip is to temporarily reduce grid size for fine adjustment, then restore it for bulk placement. Practice: enable grid snapping, move a floor tile so its origin snaps to the world grid, then rotate a wall 90 degrees with angle snapping enabled. Verify in the World Outliner that positions are clean numeric values, not fractional centimeters. Snapping makes your level feel professional and reduces time spent fixing alignment errors later.

keyIdea.title: Precision tooling
keyIdea.text: Enable snapping to lock moves, rotations, and scales to predictable increments; essential for modular and architectural scenes.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Snapping
Snapping types
  • Grid Snapping — locks translation to grid increments.
  • Angle Snapping — rotates by fixed degrees.
  • Scale Snapping — enforces consistent scale steps.
Practical guidance
Match grid size to your modular mesh dimensions to prevent gaps between tiles.
Use angle snapping for symmetry and tiled rotation increments.
Toggle snapping only when you need fine control to avoid unintended alignment jumps.
Key Takeaway
Snapping removes small errors and ensures modular assets meet cleanly — essential for production-ready levels.

screens.title: Pivot points and temporary pivot moves
screens.subtitle: Change an Actor’s pivot to rotate or scale around a specific point

narration.text: A pivot point is the origin for rotations and scales for an Actor. By default it sits at a mesh’s geometric center or a location defined by the asset, but you can temporarily move it to perform targeted rotations or scaling. For example, to simulate a door hinge, select the door Actor, hold Alt and middle-click near the hinge to temporarily move the pivot to that edge, then rotate. The door will rotate around the hinge rather than the geometric center. To make a persistent pivot change, use Ctrl+Alt with middle-click or the pivot editing tools in the Editor. A practical scenario: you have a long wall that needs to swing from one end — moving the pivot to the corner gives a natural hinged motion. Common mistakes include forgetting to reset to the default pivot, then performing future transforms with the temporary pivot still applied; be sure to reset after the operation. Also be mindful that pivot manipulations affect subsequent rotations and scales until reset. Practice moving a wall’s pivot to a corner, rotate to mimic a door, then reset the pivot and confirm the transform values return to expected behavior. Using pivot moves thoughtfully unlocks realistic localized animations and precise placement operations.

keyIdea.title: Pivot control
keyIdea.text: Move the pivot temporarily (Alt + MMB) or persistently (Ctrl + Alt + MMB) to rotate or scale around non-central points like hinges.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Pivot Points
Why pivot matters
Pivot defines center of rotation and scaling. Move it to simulate hinges or localized transformations.
Temporary pivot: Alt + Middle Mouse Button to reposition for a single operation.
Persistent pivot: Ctrl + Alt + Middle Mouse Button for longer edits.
Practice
Select a wall Actor, move pivot to a corner using Alt+MMB, rotate to mimic a door, then reset the pivot and rotate again to compare behaviors.
Example
Rotating a door around its hinge requires moving the pivot to the hinge location; otherwise rotation looks wrong.

screens.title: Hands-on lab: Build a simple room
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step: floor, walls, chair/table parenting, lights, snapping, and pivot demo

narration.text: This lab walks you through a compact scene so you can practice all the editor skills covered. Start with a blank level. Step 1: Open the Content Browser and drag SM_Floor_400x400 into the scene and set its transform to 0,0,0. Enable grid snapping and ensure the floor aligns to the grid. Step 2: Drag SM_Wall_400x200 assets to form the room walls; use the W key to move and E to rotate, applying grid and angle snapping to get exact 90-degree corners. Step 3: From Starter Content > Props, drag an SM_TableRound and an SM_Chair into the room. In the World Outliner, drag the chair onto the table to make the chair a child of the table; move the table and confirm the chair follows. Step 4: From the Place Actors panel, add a Point Light and position it above the room. Select the wall Actor, open Details, use Add Component to add a Spot Light Component, then adjust intensity and cone angle to see the effect. Step 5: Select one wall, hold Alt + Middle Mouse Button and reposition the pivot to a corner, then rotate to simulate a hinged door opening. After each step save the level and verify results in the World Outliner and Details Panel. This hands-on sequence reinforces adding Actors, component attachment, parenting, snapping, and pivot manipulation in a single, repeatable lab.

keyIdea.title: Lab summary
keyIdea.text: Build a room, parent props to demonstrate hierarchy, attach a Spot Light Component, use snapping to align, and move the pivot to hinge a wall.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Lab Walkthrough
Step sequence
  1. Drag SM_Floor_400x400 to origin and enable grid snapping.
  2. Add SM_Wall_400x200 pieces and rotate them into place with angle snapping.
  3. Place SM_TableRound and SM_Chair; parent chair to table in World Outliner.
  4. Add a Point Light from Place Actors; position and set attenuation.
  5. Select a wall, Add Component → Spot Light, change intensity and cone angle.
  6. Use Alt + MMB to move pivot to a corner and rotate the wall as a hinge.
Checkpoints
Checkpoint: Move the table; the chair should follow as a child.
Checkpoint: Toggle grid snapping; the walls should keep clean edges when snapping is on.
Checkpoint: After pivot move, the wall rotates around the new point like a door.
Why this lab
This compact project ties together placement, hierarchy, component attachment, and transform precision so you can apply the same techniques in larger levels.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three core points to keep front of mind

narration.text: Summarizing the essentials helps you retain what matters. First: Actors are the things you place in a level. They hold transforms and references to their Components. Second: Components are modular building blocks that add visuals, collision, lighting, camera functionality, or movement; compose Components to define an Actor’s runtime behavior. Third: Transform tools — the gizmo, snapping, and pivot controls — let you position and animate objects precisely. When you combine these three ideas you can build complex, maintainable scene objects that behave predictably. A frequent quality-check is to move a parent Actor and ensure children follow, confirm Components are listed in the Details Panel, and verify that modular assets align to the world grid when snapping is enabled. Keep these concepts in mind as the basis for building Blueprints and more advanced gameplay objects.

keyIdea.title: Summary Takeaway
keyIdea.text: Actors + Components + precise transforms = predictable, maintainable scene construction.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Key Concepts
Actor
The placeable container with a transform that holds Components and scripts.
Component
A reusable module you attach to an Actor to provide mesh, light, collision, camera, or movement.
Transforms & Snapping
Gizmo, grid and angle snapping, and pivot controls let you position and animate precisely.
Bottom line
Plan Actors as containers, attach focused Components, and use transform tools so your scenes are robust, editable, and easy to extend.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders for everyday use

narration.text: Use this quick reference as you work in the editor. Remember: first, always identify whether a change requires a new Actor or just a Component property change. Second, name and parent objects deliberately to prevent orphaning elements and to make reparenting easier when you iterate. Third, enable snapping and manage pivot moves when precision is required; these small habits save hours of cleanup. When you run into unexpected behavior, check the World Outliner for parent-child relationships and the Details Panel for Components; many errors come from accidental detachment or misapplied properties. Keep these three checks as part of your build routine. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means ask: actor or component? is the parent correct? is snapping/pivot set for precision?. In practical terms, three compact reminders for everyday use. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Ask: Actor or Component? Is the parent correct? Is snapping/pivot set for precision?

Actor vs Component
Decide if you need a new Actor or just a Component change.
Naming & Parentage

Final thought
Small editor habits — naming, checking parentage, and using snapping — produce more reliable levels and faster iteration.
